title: Snapshot Radio SLAM: Initial Pose and Clock

meta.author: Bai Liping
meta.subject: Unified angle-delay snapshot radio SLAM, conditional least squares, SVD and orientation estimation

slides.notes:
This public educational deck explains the method in arXiv:2607.04847v2. The paper uses estimated path delays and angles to initialize a known-BS, unknown-UE radio SLAM problem. It does not assume an initial UE state. The early linear solve is conditional on an orientation candidate. The browser laboratories expose geometry, the conditional linear system and orientation optimization. They are deliberately smaller than the full exhaustive-subset plus IRLS/QAIC estimator. All prose and teaching examples here are explanatory rather than copied paper text.

Sources:
Paper · abstract — https://arxiv.org/html/2607.04847v2
Radio measurements → radio map — https://bailiping.com/mpc-detection-to-bounce-count-slides/

slides.notes:
The input is a set of noisy channel-parameter estimates. The estimator discussed here does not operate directly on raw IQ samples. The paper assumes known BS position and orientation, which anchors the global coordinate frame. In 3D, pose means three position coordinates and three rotation degrees of freedom, with an additional clock bias. The observation vector contains one range-like delay and two angular pairs. Path magnitudes are deliberately not used by the proposed estimator. Noise covariance is part of the simulator, but calibrated per-path covariance is not an estimator input.

Sources:
Section II-A · Eqs. (1)–(3) — https://arxiv.org/html/2607.04847v2#S2.SS1

slides.notes:
B is a teaching and implementation notation for c times the clock bias. The original paper keeps b in seconds and stacks minus c b in its linear unknown vector. This deck will show that exact sign convention before relating it to the positive-B convention used by the browser. A positive receiver timing offset adds to every measured delay. The geometry, not an independent per-path clock correction, must separate propagation lengths from that common offset. The simulator can set a true clock to generate data, but that truth is never given to an unknown-state estimator.

This slide gives a short algebraic explanation equivalent to the paper’s auxiliary-segment derivation. Multiplying t=a u-s v by M yields a(v-u)-s(u-v)=(a+s)(v-u). The stated M follows Eq. (10). slides.notes:
The residual is a vector in metres, since M and w are dimensionless and both t and corrected path length are distances. The paper minimizes the sum of squared residual norms at the coarse stage. A residual near zero is geometric consistency with the eliminated model, not an automatic proof of a positive-length physical path or correct path identity. The later consensus and feasibility checks handle outliers and inadmissible candidates. A fixed orientation creates a linear least-squares subproblem, but an unknown orientation still requires search or nonlinear optimization.

slides.notes:
Each path contributes a three-row block, but its rows need not represent three independent constraints. The 3D matrix has four columns for the three displacement coordinates and one signed distance-clock coordinate. The planar construction retains the 3D embedding and adds a row fixing vertical displacement to zero. It is equivalent to eliminating the fixed vertical coordinate algebraically. The pseudoinverse produces a least-squares solution for noisy data and a minimum-norm solution if the matrix is rank deficient. Rank must therefore be inspected rather than inferred from the number of rows.

slides.notes:
Profiling means eliminating position and clock by their exact conditional least-squares solution before comparing orientations. This is a lower-dimensional nonlinear problem. In planar mode, the paper samples the heading circle at one-degree resolution. In full 3D, a yaw-only curve is a slice of SO(3), not an exhaustive rotation search. The residual also has nonphysical and ambiguous algebraic configurations, which is why feasibility and rank checks remain necessary. The browser’s local refinement is an educational optimization experiment and should be read with its stated initialization.

slides.notes:
Equations (25)–(27) use a left perturbation R_new=Exp([delta omega]_cross)R. Stack each 3-by-3 J_R,i block and each three-vector residual before solving delta omega=-J_R dagger r. The Jacobian on this slide differentiates the coarse residual r=M t-d(v-u) with respect to a rotation perturbation while holding t and d fixed. It is not a total derivative of the profiled objective through t_hat(R) and B_hat(R). After updating orientation, the paper resolves the linear position-and-clock block and repeats. The minus sign follows from minimizing r+J_R delta. This is distinct from the later physical refinement convention e=z-h with J=dh/dTheta, where the increment has the positive weighted-pseudoinverse form. Step control and convergence thresholds are numerical implementation choices.

slides.notes:
The paper selects a twist from its yaw grid and then traverses swing-axis and swing-magnitude candidates around that one twist seed. Its experimental spacings are 6 degrees for twist, 12 for swing axis, 10 for swing magnitude and a 90-degree maximum swing. The subsequent left-multiplicative exponential update preserves a valid rotation matrix. A single selected twist can miss another orientation basin, and local Gauss–Newton refinement is not globally convergent. The browser lab demonstrates a yaw slice and local SO(3) mechanics. It is not the complete paper twist-swing plus exhaustive-subset plus IRLS/QAIC implementation.

slides.notes:
Section IV analyzes the rank of this particular eliminated residual. The matrix M has rank two for a generic single-bounce path and rank one at LoS. The clock column does not increase the translation-plus-clock block rank for one path. In the full residual, a single-bounce path has at most two independent first-order constraints in 3D, leading to a minimum of four paths for seven local state coordinates. In planar mode the full per-path residual has at most one independent local constraint at a true inlier, leading to four for four unknowns. These are formulation-specific necessary implications, not universal minimum measurement counts for all radio positioning methods. At LoS truth the coarse orientation derivative vanishes, unlike the full physical angle model.

Sources:
Section IV · Theorem 1 and minimal sets — https://arxiv.org/html/2607.04847v2#S4
Planar analysis · Section IV-B — https://arxiv.org/html/2607.04847v2#S4.SS2

slides.notes:
The published procedure is exhaustive minimum-subset consensus with an MSAC-style truncated squared residual objective. It is not necessary to call it randomized RANSAC, since every minimum-size subset is enumerated in Algorithm 1. The winning hypothesis minimizes the truncated cost, and its thresholded residuals define the coarse inlier set. In the experiments T_epsilon is one metre because the vector residual has distance units. A random subset cap is an implementation approximation that must be disclosed. The browser labs do not perform this robust outer search.

slides.notes:
The square root of W premultiplies both the Jacobian and residual in the least-squares step. Using W directly there would square the intended weight. Because W_jj is the inverse row norm, the actual row multiplier is the inverse square root of that norm. The weights are recomputed at each linearization and then held fixed for the local solve. The paper distinguishes this row-equilibrated IRLS method from minimization of a calibrated Gaussian likelihood. Numerical row floors, line-search choices, stopping rules and the units used for state coordinates affect an implementation and must be documented. Local rotation increments use a left exponential update.

\[\delta_\ell=(\mathbf W_\ell^{1/2}\mathbf J_\ell)^\dagger\mathbf W_\ell^{1/2}\mathbf e_\ell\]Add Euclidean increments.

slides.notes:
All M+1 candidate models are refined before selecting the smallest QAIC score. The terminal weighted residual is a quasi-deviance, not an exact negative log-likelihood, because its weights come from Jacobian row equilibration. The dimension count uses genuine degrees of freedom: 4 planar UE coordinates or 7 spatial UE coordinates, plus 2 or 3 per modeled single-bounce scatterer. It does not count nine rotation-matrix entries as nine free parameters. The paper sets the residual scale to exp(gamma) at the simulated noise level, not to the constant Euler number. Logarithms at zero residual require an explicit numerical safeguard.

elements.html: QAIC compares the refined candidate models
Fit quality and model dimension determine the selected LoS hypothesis.
\[\widetilde E_m=\|\mathbf W_m^{1/2}\mathbf e_m\|_2^2\]\[\mathrm{QAIC}_m=2d_\Theta^{(m)}+\frac{n}{\hat c}\ln\!\left(\frac{\widetilde E_m}{n}\right)\]\[n=k_dM,\quad k_d=3\ \text{or}\ 5\]

Residual term: how well the candidate explains the observations.

Dimension term: a LoS path needs no scatterer, so its model has fewer parameters.

Experiments use \(\hat c=\exp(\gamma)\).
This scale is a tuning choice.

arXiv:2607.04847v2 robustly rejects paths inconsistent with LoS or one-bounce geometry. Its Appendix B synthetic multi-bounce outliers use random angles and skew-normal delays rather than ray-traced double-bounce scenes. No claim is made that its residual classifies every physical path’s bounce count correctly. A replication should expose missing seeds, unspecified feasibility thresholds and numerical conventions, and should report unconditional performance rather than dropping failed solves. The three embedded labs teach selected stages and do not constitute the entire algorithm.

elements.html: What this method does with double-bounce paths
In this paper, multi-bounce paths are outliers to reject.

LoS: one straight segment.

Single bounce: two segments meeting at one unknown point.

Double bounce generally needs two interaction points and three segment lengths. It does not satisfy this single-scatterer model.
WHAT TO CHECK IN A REPLICATION

Retain failed trials and report them.

Inspect rank, conditioning and physical feasibility.

State orientation initialization and numerical choices.

Local convergence and a low residual do not guarantee the correct global solution.
